title: Artificial versus Natural Atoms: The uncanny capability of the many-body Schrödinger equation to produce emergent behavior
abstract: The paper reviews the theoretical and experimental progress achieved in the last 25 years in understanding the novel physics of artificial atoms and molecules as arising from the formation of Wigner molecules (WMs) of localized (to a stronger or lesser extent) fermionic or bosonic particles, which are finite quantum analogs of the more familiar bulk Wigner crystal. The term artificial atoms, as used here, encompasses a broad range of recently fabricated quantum nanodevices and experimental apparatuses consisting of a finite number of mutually repelling confined particles, including two-dimensional semiconductor and moiré transition metal dichalcogenide quantum dots, as well as trapped ultracold neutral atoms or ions. These nano-sized or micro-sized artificial devices and apparatuses (in single well or multi-well of variable-shape arrangements) hold a great promise for technological applications in the field of quantum information and quantum computers, as well as for advances in fundamental many-body physics. Prominent quantum effects of Wigner molecularization are the strong quenching of the spectral energy gaps, the appearance of rovibational spectra (in analogy with natural molecules), entanglement, and pinning due to an external perturbation. In high magnetic fields or at rapid rotation, WMs provide an alternative theory to the fractional quantum Hall effect. The physics of Wigner molecules is shown to derive from the solutions of the many-body Schrödinger equation (MBSE) in the regime of strong interparticle correlations arising from the dominance of the potential over the kinetic energy, or from a high magnetic field, as well as from a rapid rotation... summary: This review surveys the novel physics of artificial atoms formed by strongly correlated particles, known as Wigner molecules. It demonstrates how the many-body Schrödinger equation predicts emergent quantum phenomena, such as molecular-like spectra, when interparticle repulsion dominates kinetic energy. The work is highly relevant for understanding correlated electron behavior in nanoscale quantum devices and trapped quantum simulators.
main_problem: The paper reviews the physics of 'artificial atoms' and molecules, which are finite quantum analogs of Wigner crystals, arising from strongly interacting, confined particles.
main_result: The physics is governed by the many-body Schrödinger equation (MBSE) in regimes of strong interparticle correlations, leading to emergent phenomena like rovibronal spectra and Wigner molecularization.
method: The review synthesizes theoretical calculations (e.g., FCI, symmetry projection) and discusses experimental platforms, focusing on the Wigner parameter to characterize the correlation strength.
model_or_system: The systems include 2D semiconductor/moiré quantum dots, trapped ultracold atoms/ions, and electron clusters under high magnetic fields or rotation. The underlying physics is described by the MBSE for mutually repelling confined particles.
key_observables: Spectral energy gaps, rovibronal spectra, entanglement, and pinning effects.
important_parameters: The Wigner parameter (RW = Potential Energy / Kinetic Energy) and external fields like magnetic field (B) and rotation ($\Omega$).
main_assumptions: The analysis develops a view of symmetry breaking based exclusively on finite systems, contrasting with the thermodynamic limit.
paper_structure: The review progresses from general concepts of Wigner molecularization to specific computational methods (e.g., hierarchical schemes) and details results across different physical regimes (field-free, magnetic field, rotating traps).
why_interesting: It bridges the gap between fundamental many-body theory (MBSE) and modern experimental platforms (quantum dots, trapped atoms) to study emergent quantum behavior in strongly correlated systems.
